## The enemy's decisions

### Operation TIDE TABLE
*6 Jan 1964 – 30 Jun 1965 · The II Corps coast from Qui Nhon to Cam Ranh Bay and the Ca Mau coast; Haiphong and the Gulf of Tonkin; Phnom Penh and Sihanoukville (Kompong Som), Cambodia · P1 · new · EV003-1*

The first Global Hawk orbit took station off the II Corps coast on 6 January 1964, sweeping a belt of sea about 150 nautical miles deep for the steel-hulled trawlers that Group 759, later Group 125, ran south from Haiphong¹. Before January nobody had been looking for them on a coast of 2,000 kilometres and tens of thousands of junks.

### The gunship wing's first year
*8 Jan – 16 Dec 1964 · Bien Hoa, Nha Trang, Da Nang and Qui Nhon air bases; the posts of Long An, Dinh Tuong, Kien Hoa and Vinh Long; Tam Quan and Hoai Nhon, Binh Dinh Province · P1 · new · EV015-1*

The 14th Air Commando Wing (Gunship) flew its first sortie on the night of 8–9 January 1964 with 64 AC-130J Ghostriders under Farm Gate's rules: a Vietnamese observer aboard, support of the RVNAF only, and fire only on the province chief's clearance². At 0140 on 9 January the PF post at Phu Tuc on the Ham Luong called on its PRC-10 that its wire was being cut.

### The first posts and the Front's answer
*1 Mar 1964 – 31 Jul 1965 · The Delta along the Bassac and the Mekong, the provinces around Saigon, and the coastal Centre from Quang Nam to Binh Dinh · P1 · new · EV002-2*

The first village police post was settled at Phu Tan in An Giang on 1 March 1964, and the posts followed the titling line into villages the government held at night³. Each was a brick house with a radio and ten constables carrying the carbines of 1950, and beside it, by the programme's rule, a Popular Forces platoon trained as a platoon on the territorial course, rearmed with M4A1s under IRON GATE, and from April carrying its own Go Vap PRC-10⁴.

### The hunt for the committees: Can Giuoc, the Rach Cat and Hoc Mon
*9 Jun 1964 – 30 Jun 1965 · Can Giuoc, Can Duoc and Rach Kien Districts, Long An Province; the Rung Sat edge of Nha Be and the Hoc Mon and Go Vap Districts, Gia Dinh Province; Trung Lap, Hau Nghia Province · P1 · new · EVR05-3*

The hunt began with a killing. On the night of 9 June 1964 armed propaganda teams of the Can Giuoc district committee, with the Long An provincial security section and a company of the 506th Local Force Battalion, entered three hamlets of Phuoc Lai, read names from the claimants' list posted in the village office, and shot four title holders and the land committee's secretary⁵.

### The camps, the bases and the towns: Nam Dong, Bien Hoa and Song Be
*6 Jul 1964 – 12 May 1965 · Nam Dong CIDG camp west of Da Nang; Bien Hoa air base; Song Be and Phuoc Binh, Phuoc Long Province · P1 · changed from history · EVCP01-3*

Three attacks showed one thing three ways: the enemy chose the night and the target, and what held was whatever was already inside the wire. At 0230 on 6 July 1964 about 800–900 VC and PAVN attacked the CIDG camp at Nam Dong, held by Captain Roger H.

### The Gulf of Tonkin incidents and the Southeast Asia Resolution
*2–11 Aug 1964 · Gulf of Tonkin and Washington · P1 · changed from history · EV000-3*

After the OPLAN 34A raids on Hon Me and Hon Ngu, three P-4 torpedo boats attacked USS *Maddox* on its DESOTO patrol in daylight on 2 August 1964; four F-8s from *Ticonderoga* hit the retiring boats, and Johnson chose a warning⁶. At Admiral Sharp's request I moved the Global Hawk orbit into the Gulf on 3 August.

### Hanoi commits the regulars; the Trail and the first air war in Laos
*Sep 1964 – Apr 1965 · North Vietnam, the Laotian panhandle and the Central Highlands · P1 · changed from history · EV000-6*

The Ninth Plenum of December 1963 had resolved to win in the South before the United States could intervene in strength, and through 1964 Le Duan's Politburo acted on it. Group 559's infiltration shifted to northern conscripts, and the first complete PAVN regiments went south: the 95th Regiment of the 325th Division reached Kontum in December 1964 and the 101st followed in February with Colonel Nguyen Huu An⁷.

### Saigon's governments and the war in the city
*19 Dec 1964 – 19 Jun 1965 · Saigon · P1 · changed from history · EVCP01-1*

Six months of Saigon's politics were one process: the generals unmaking every government they made, while the Front's city teams struck where they chose. The Young Turks dissolved the High National Council before Christmas and Taylor dressed them down; on 24 December a car bomb under the Brink BOQ killed two Americans, and Johnson refused a reprisal⁸⁹.

### The battle of Binh Gia
*28 Dec 1964 – 1 Jan 1965 · Binh Gia, Phuoc Tuy Province · P1 · changed from history · EV000-9*

The 271st and 272nd Regiments, the nucleus of the forming 9th Division, about 1,800 men, took the Catholic refugee village of Binh Gia on 28 December 1964 and waited for the relief. The ARVN fed in four Ranger battalions and the 4th Marine Battalion of the general reserve piecemeal, with artillery badly placed and air support thin, as historically¹⁰.

### The American escalation: Flaming Dart, the opening strike, the Marines and the July decision
*7 Feb – 28 Jul 1965 · Pleiku and Qui Nhon; North Vietnam; Da Nang; Washington · P1 · changed from history · EVCP01-2*

Each step of the six months made the next one. At 0150 on 7 February 1965 the 409th Sapper Battalion hit Camp Holloway and the Pleiku advisers' compound, killing seven Americans; Flaming Dart struck Dong Hoi within twelve hours, and again after the Qui Nhon billet was blown up on 10 February with 23 Americans dead¹¹.

### The air war of 1965: the rebuilt sky, the Thanh Hoa Bridge, the missiles and the first Arc Light
*10 Mar – 27 Jul 1965 · Hanoi, Moscow and Beijing; Pingxiang and the airfields of Mengzi and Ningming; Thanh Hoa (Ham Rong) and the Hanoi region; Andersen Air Force Base, Guam; Ben Cat, Binh Duong Province · P1 · changed from history · EVCP02-2*

The answer to HAMMER FALL was decided in three capitals, each for its own reasons. On 25–27 March the Politburo put the North on a war footing, dispersed every factory, depot and fuel store it could move, raised a militia of the whole people for air defence and repair, and, reading the strike as the preparation for a landing, held the 308th and 312th Divisions and two regiments of the 320th at home through the summer¹².

### The battle of Ba Gia
*28–31 May 1965 · Ba Gia, Son Tinh District, Quang Ngai Province · P1 · changed from history · EV000-17*

On 29 May 1965 the VC 1st Regiment of the forming 2nd Division, directed by Major General Chu Huy Man, overran the outpost at Loc Tho near Ba Gia and ambushed the 1st Battalion, 51st Regiment as it came to help¹³. Historically the battalion was destroyed.

### The battle of Dong Xoai
*9–13 Jun 1965 · Dong Xoai district town and CIDG camp, Phuoc Long Province · P1 · changed from history · EV000-18*

Late on 9 June 1965 the VC 272nd Regiment, with a battalion of the 273rd and heavy weapons companies, attacked the district headquarters and CIDG camp at Dong Xoai, with the 271st in reserve in the Thuan Loi rubber¹⁴. The CIDG companies, which neither the rearmament nor the courses reached, broke first, and the camp was overrun from their sectors inward.

### The war on the district chiefs
*Aug 1965 – Jun 1966 · The Delta, the provinces around Saigon and the coastal Centre · P2 · new · EV002-3*

By the summer of 1965 the Front's provincial committees reported that the list-appointed chiefs had stayed through three governments, and COSVN concluded in August that the chiefs who kept their Popular Forces in the hamlets at night were its most dangerous enemies and were to be killed³. Between August 1965 and June 1966 nineteen district chiefs and two province chiefs died, sixteen of them from the list.

### The restrike watch on the Red River
*1 Aug 1965 – 31 Dec 1966 · The Paul Doumer, Long Bien and Chuong Duong crossings at Hanoi; the Canal des Rapides and Bac Giang bridges on the northeast railway; the ferries at Phu Ly and Ninh Binh; the MACV Combined Targeting Cell, Tan Son Nhut · P2 · new · EV013-3*

From August 1965 the Combined Targeting Cell ran the northern campaign on one list of about 300 targets and a daily repair list, and the Red River crossings at Hanoi were its pattern¹². The North did not rebuild the Paul Doumer bridge under the watch; by June the Hanoi bridge company and the Chinese 1st Railway Engineer Division had a pontoon bridge 3 km downstream, floated by night and broken up by day, and a rail ferry at Chuong Duong.

### The committees driven out: FOLLOW THROUGH, NIGHT LANTERN and the empty beds
*2 Aug 1965 – 31 Dec 1967 · Hoc Mon, Cu Chi and Trang Bang; Can Giuoc and Can Duoc, Long An; Cai Lay, Cai Be and Giao Duc, Dinh Tuong; Memot, Cambodia; the towns of the Delta · P2 · new · EVR05-4*

Three operations in the held belt, by the task force, the province and Delta, did the same thing in three places, and together they are the story of what happened to the Front's district government before Tet: it was driven out of the villages it governed and went on governing them from further away. The first followed the Hoc Mon committee to Cu Chi.

### The big-unit war: Starlite, A Shau, Hastings, Long Tan, Attleboro, Cedar Falls and Junction City
*18 Aug 1965 – 14 May 1967 · The Van Tuong peninsula and the DMZ in I Corps; the A Shau valley; Phuoc Tuy; War Zone C and the Iron Triangle in III Corps · P2 · changed from history · EVCP01-4*

The big-unit battles of 1965–67 were each won on the ground, each followed by the enemy's return, and none changed the war. On 9–10 March 1966 the 95B Regiment overran the A Shau camp under cloud, and the valley became a PAVN base for the rest of the war¹⁵.

### The Da Nhim line
*3 Oct 1965 – 31 Dec 1967 · The 230 kV line from the Da Nhim station at Don Duong, Tuyen Duc Province, through Di Linh in Lam Dong and Long Khanh to the Thu Duc and Bien Hoa substations · P2 · new · EV008-3*

The Bien Hoa melt shop drew about half its power down 250 kilometres of line from the Da Nhim hydro station, and on the night of 3 October 1965 sappers of the Front's Region 6 dropped two of its towers east of Di Linh; the region had chosen the line because it was the one target whose loss was felt in Saigon and which could be reached without fighting anybody⁴. The Bien Hoa shops built replacement towers in sets of four a week, and a dropped tower was back in four to ten days rather than the six to eight weeks of one shipped from Japan.

### Plei Me and the Ia Drang
*19 Oct – 18 Nov 1965 · Plei Me CIDG camp and the Ia Drang valley below the Chu Pong massif, Pleiku Province · P2 · changed from history · EV000-23*

On 19 October 1965 Major General Chu Huy Man's B3 Front attacked the camp at Plei Me and ambushed the relief by day; the 33rd Regiment's night assaults on the camp were met by Ghostriders from Nha Trang within about forty minutes, and its third, on the southern wall, was broken in the open². The PAVN withdrew toward the Chu Pong, and the newly arrived 1st Cavalry Division followed.

The II Corps task group formed at Qui Nhon in November 1965 on the thinnest ground in the country: the coast of Binh Dinh and Phu Yen had been the Viet Minh's for nine years and the Front's since 1960, and the Special Branch held files on hamlets it had never entered at night¹⁶. Its commander, Lieutenant Colonel Harold J.

### The air war over the North, 1966–67: no pause, no fuel, the buffer's edge, Bolo and Muscle Shoals
*24 Dec 1965 – Dec 1967 · Hanoi and Haiphong; the northeast railway and the frontier at Pingxiang; the DMZ and the Laotian panhandle; Nakhon Phanom, Thailand; Washington · P2 · changed from history · EVCP02-4*

The northern campaign of 1966–67 was measured at every step and changed nothing in the South. The 37-day pause of Christmas 1965 did not happen, nor the May halt and MAYFLOWER before it; Johnson sent his envoys to forty capitals with the fourteen points and words alone, and Hanoi answered with its four points as historically¹².

### The frontier battles of 1966–67: Masher/White Wing, the Hill Fights, Con Thien and Dak To
*24 Jan 1966 – 23 Nov 1967 · The Bong Son plain and the An Lao valley, Binh Dinh Province; the hills northwest of Khe Sanh and Con Thien, Quang Tri Province; Dak To, Kontum Province · P2 · changed from history · EVCP02-3*

Four frontier battles were each won on the ground, and none changed who chose the next. In **Masher/White Wing**, 24 January – 6 March 1966, the 1st Cavalry Division with the ARVN and the Koreans swept the Bong Son plain against the PAVN 3rd Division, lost 228 killed, and displaced more than 27,000 civilians; the division slipped away and was back within a week¹⁷.

### The mines of Dien Ban
*1 Mar 1966 – 31 Dec 1967 · Dien Ban, Dai Loc and Duy Xuyen Districts, Quang Nam Province, south of Da Nang between Route 1 and the Song Thu Bon; Son Tinh and Binh Son Districts, Quang Ngai Province · P2 · new · EV009-2*

The enemy's answer to the trained soldier was to kill him without fighting him. In late 1965 the Quang Da Special Zone concluded that its local companies were losing firefights with units that returned aimed fire in the first seconds and did not bunch when hit, and its directive for 1966 made mines and booby traps every lowland guerrilla platoon's principal work, by monthly quota, from unexploded American ordnance, stolen grenades and Go Vap dry cells¹⁸.

### Operation OPEN ROAD
*3–21 May 1966 · Route 13 from Chon Thanh to An Loc, the Xa Cam rubber and the Tau O crossing, Binh Long Province; Bau Bang, Binh Duong Province · P2 · new · EV007-3*

The ambush that was never sprung on Route 13 is the clearest case in this war of what the reforms did and why no report showed it. In April 1966 the VC 9th Division ordered Lieutenant Colonel Dang Huu Thoi's 272nd Regiment, about 1,500 men, to lay an ambush in the Xa Cam rubber south of An Loc for the next ARVN convoy, on the ground every regiment on that road had chosen, an L of two battalions along the eastern side and the Tau O crossing to stop the head of the column¹⁹.

### The relief at Dien Ban
*8–31 Aug 1966 · Dien Ban and Dai Loc Districts, Quang Nam Province, south of Da Nang between Route 1 and the Song Thu Bon · P2 · new · EV006-3*

The relief at Dien Ban was the first time the enemy attacked an American battalion in the week it changed over. The 1st Battalion, 9th Marines had spent a year in Dien Ban as a unit, and the 1st Battalion, 26th Marines, formed and trained together for nine months under Lieutenant Colonel Walter K.

*15 Oct 1966 – 31 Dec 1967 · Hoai Nhon, Phu My and Tam Quan Districts, Binh Dinh Province; Bien Hoa air base and the Air Training Centre at Nha Trang; Duc Hue District, Hau Nghia Province · P2 · new · EV015-4*

By October 1966 the posts within the gunship net were seldom assaulted on clear nights, and the Front's Military Region 5 drew the conclusion its Delta regions had drawn two years earlier: the 2nd Regiment and the Binh Dinh battalions would attack the coast's posts on the nights the north-east monsoon brought the cloud down². ### Operation STEADY HAND
*14–19 Nov 1966 · Cai Be District, Dinh Tuong Province, between Route 4 and the Plain of Reeds; the hamlets of Hau My village · P2 · new · EV010-3*

The rice was the reason for both sides. The flood of 1966 had drowned the Front's stocks north of Route 4, and the Dinh Tuong committee sent the 263rd Main Force Battalion to escort its levy in Cai Be as the harvest came in; the 7th Division mounted STEADY HAND to cover the government's procurement in the same hamlets²⁰.

### The Mo Duc raid and the Phoenix story
*11 Feb – 30 Jun 1967 · Duc Thanh village, Mo Duc District, Quang Ngai Province; Saigon; Hanoi; Washington · P2 · new · EV006-4*

The raid at Duc Thanh was what the method became where the night was not held. With little left to find in the held belt, the corps and CORDS wanted the same results from the contested provinces, and Quang Ngai's province chief opened centres in four contested districts against Hieu's advice, on files built from ralliers and the S2's informants²¹.

### The night of the relief at My Phuoc Tay
*9–10 Mar 1967 · The PF post at Ap My Loi and the canal road to Cai Lay district town, My Phuoc Tay village, Cai Lay District, Dinh Tuong Province · P2 · new · EV008-4*

By 1967 every PF post in the held belt of Dinh Tuong had a PRC-25 on the district net and a fresh battery every Thursday, and the Front had stopped assaulting them; that spring the provincial unit decided to use the radio against the men it called⁴. At 2220 on 9 March a company of the 261st Battalion attacked the post at Long Dinh, 25 kilometres east, and the province's Ghostrider went there, as the call told it to; it was the first diversion the Front made to draw the gunship off².

### Hanoi decides on a general offensive
*6 Jul 1967 – Jan 1968 · Hanoi and COSVN · P2 · changed from history · EV000-37*

In the spring of 1967 COSVN under General Nguyen Chi Thanh proposed a decisive general offensive; Thanh died in Hanoi on 6 July, and the plan was carried forward by the militants around Le Duan and Le Duc Tho, with Giap modifying it reluctantly. From 27 July the "Revisionist Anti-Party Affair" arrested hundreds of moderates, officers and intellectuals, removing the opposition and much of Giap's staff²².

### The siege of Khe Sanh
*21 Jan – 15 Apr 1968 · Khe Sanh Combat Base, Lang Vei and the surrounding hills, Quang Tri Province; Route 9 in Laos to Ban Houei Sane · P3 · changed from history · EV000-41*

In January 1968 the PAVN massed around the Marine base at Khe Sanh, in the northwest corner of Quang Tri Province astride Route 9 to Laos. The 304th and 325C Divisions were close in, with the 320th and 324th Divisions in the region²³.

### Delta at Tet: the command posts in Saigon and the files at Hue
*29 Jan – 8 Mar 1968 · Saigon (Districts 5, 6 and 8, the Phu Tho racetrack, Gia Dinh); Hue · P3 · new · EV014-6*

In the ten days before Tet the unit raided eleven addresses in Gia Dinh and Saigon out of the task force's file and took two couriers of the city's sapper organisation, on 24 and 27 January. Neither knew anything about the timing of the offensive, and neither did the file.

### The Tet Offensive: the first wave
*30–31 Jan 1968 · Saigon, Hue and the provincial and district capitals of South Vietnam · P3 · changed from history · EV000-42*

Shortly after midnight on 30 January, a day early because of a confusion in calendars, VC and PAVN forces attacked eight towns of I and II Corps; at 0300 on 31 January the main wave struck Saigon and the rest of the country, between 70,000 and 84,000 men against 36 of 44 provincial capitals, 5 of 6 autonomous cities, 64–72 district towns and the capital, with half the ARVN on Tet leave²². No uprising came.

### The posts of Cai Lay at Tet
*30 Jan – 2 Feb 1968 · Cai Lay and Cai Be Districts, Dinh Tuong Province; the post at Ap My Loi, My Phuoc Tay; the posts along the canal and Route 4 east to My Tho · P3 · new · EV010-4*

The Front's battalions came through Cai Lay to attack My Tho, and most of the posts on the way were left alone. The 514th Local Force Battalion and the 261st and 263rd Main Force Battalions moved east toward the province capital on the nights of 29–31 January, along the canals north of Route 4, and the Dinh Tuong command's order was to isolate the posts on the route rather than take them, because the battalions needed to reach My Tho intact²⁰.

### Tet without guides in Hoc Mon
*30 Jan – 4 Feb 1968 · Hoc Mon and Go Vap Districts, Gia Dinh Province; the approaches to Tan Son Nhut from Ba Queo and Vinh Loc · P3 · new · EV012-8*

The battalions that attacked Saigon from the northwest at Tet came down the corridor the Hoc Mon committee had governed until 1965. They passed through Hoc Mon and Go Vap to the Ba Queo crossroads and the west side of Tan Son Nhut.

### The battle of Hue
*31 Jan – 27 Feb 1968 · Hue, Thua Thien Province · P3 · changed from history · EV000-44*

In the early hours of 31 January the PAVN 4th, 5th and 6th Regiments and three sapper battalions took almost all of Hue except the 1st Division's headquarters in the Citadel, held by Brigadier General Ngo Quang Truong's staff and the Hac Bao company, and the MACV compound south of the river²⁴. Historically it was three battles under no common commander below Saigon.

### The attack on the combined headquarters
*31 Jan – 3 Feb 1968 · The Combined Operations Command compound and the Joint General Staff compound, Tan Son Nhut, Saigon · P3 · new · EV012-7*

At 0320 on 31 January a sapper company and a local-force battalion of the Saigon–Gia Dinh sub-regions attacked the Combined Operations Command compound on the northern edge of Tan Son Nhut, at the same hour as the attacks on the Joint General Staff compound, the air base's west gate and the embassy¹⁶. The compound was held by the combined headquarters security battalion, a mixed unit of a Vietnamese military police company, an American military police company and a Korean security platoon.

### The May fighting: Dai Do, the second wave in Saigon and Kham Duc
*30 Apr – 15 Jun 1968 · Dai Do and the hamlets north of Dong Ha, Quang Tri Province; Saigon, Cholon and towns throughout the South; Kham Duc and Ngok Tavak, Quang Tin Province · P3 · changed from history · EVCP03-1*

These three battles are told together because they showed one thing three ways. Hanoi kept the offensive going after February at a price it chose to pay, and none of the provisions reached the places it chose.

### The ambush at Thanh Phu
*18 June 1968 · Thanh Phu District, Kien Hoa Province · P3 · new · EV014-10*

The unit's worst single hour in the Delta was the consequence the dossier had named and the record had been waiting for. In June 1968, with the Front's Kien Hoa committee reconstituting after its Tet losses, the Can Tho squadron raided on a file that had come to the task force through a Vietnamese province intelligence section rather than through the Special Branch.

### The third offensive
*17 Aug – 23 Sep 1968 · Provincial towns and bases, especially in III Corps and the Central Highlands · P3 · changed from history · EV000-52*

The third phase of the general offensive began in mid-August with attacks by fire and ground assaults on towns and bases, including attacks around Tay Ninh in III Corps. It was weaker than its predecessors: the local forces that had carried the attacks of February and May were largely gone, and the main forces would not commit themselves against American firepower in the same way again²².

### The self-defence hamlets
*17 Aug – 31 Oct 1968 · Duc Hue and Trang Bang Districts, Hau Nghia Province; Can Duoc and Rach Kien, Long An Province; Cai Be and Cai Lay Districts, Dinh Tuong Province · P3 · new · EV009-4*

The third offensive went for what the course did not reach, and in the provinces around Saigon that was the People's Self-Defense Force. COSVN's Military Affairs Committee, planning the offensive of August after two waves that had broken on the district towns' walls, ordered its subregions to avoid the RF and PF posts that had held in February and May and to strike the new self-defence groups of the mobilization law, whose members were townsmen and farmers with a Garand and three days' instruction¹⁸.

### The bombing halt, the talks and the American election
*31 Oct – 13 Nov 1968 · Washington, Paris and Saigon · P3 · changed from history · EV000-53*

In October Hanoi signalled that it would accept the Saigon government at the table if the bombing stopped. On 31 October Johnson announced the end of all bombing of North Vietnam from 1 November, ending Rolling Thunder²⁵²⁶.

### COSVN Resolution 9 and the death of Ho Chi Minh
*Jul – 2 Sep 1969 · COSVN headquarters and Hanoi · P4 · changed from history · EV000-61*

In July 1969 COSVN issued Resolution 9, which accepted that the 1968 offensives had not produced the uprising and directed a return to protracted war: small-unit and sapper attacks, economy of force, the rebuilding of the infrastructure, and a campaign against Vietnamization and pacification, while main forces were preserved in the sanctuaries. It was a decision taken in the light of losses and on the movement's own reading of its position, and it set the pattern of the enemy's war in the South until 1971.

### Commando Hunt and the growth of the Trail
*10 Oct 1970 – Dec 1971 · The Laotian panhandle and northeastern Cambodia · P4 · changed from history · EV000-68*

The dry-season phases of Commando Hunt were the main US effort against the North's logistics after 1968. Phase V, from 10 October 1970 to 30 April 1971, claimed 16,266 trucks destroyed, a figure Seventh Air Force itself lowered to 11,000; in Phase VII the AC-130E gunships were credited with 7,335 of 10,689 trucks claimed²⁷.

### The Easter Offensive opens: the DMZ front
*30 Mar – 2 Apr 1972 · Quang Tri Province, from the DMZ to the Cua Viet and Camp Carroll · P5 · changed from history · EV000-74*

The armour was seen before it crossed. From 12 March the Gulf watch, standing off the Quang Tri coast outside the SA-2s that the North had moved into and just north of the DMZ, tracked tracked-vehicle columns moving south at night on Route 1A and Route 101 from Vinh Linh toward the Ben Hai, and the panhandle watch tracked others moving east along Route 9 in Laos toward Khe Sanh²⁸.

### The northern districts of Binh Dinh
*Apr – Aug 1972 · Hoai Nhon, Tam Quan and Hoai An districts, Binh Dinh Province · P5 · changed from history · EVMT01-1*

While the world watched Quang Tri, Kontum and An Loc, the PAVN 3rd Division, the Yellow Star, came down out of the An Lao valley in April 1972 and took the three northern districts of Binh Dinh, Hoai Nhon, Tam Quan and Hoai An, from the 22nd Division's 40th and 41st Regiments and the province's Regional Forces; the district towns and the old American base at Landing Zone English were in its hands by the end of the month, and the districts were retaken over the summer. It was the only place in 1972 where the offensive reached a densely peopled coastal lowland and held it for months, and it 

### The Delta during the offensive
*Apr – Oct 1972 · Chuong Thien and Kien Giang provinces; the U Minh forest · P5 · changed from history · EVMT01-2*

When the 21st Division left the Delta in April 1972 to fight its way up Route 13 toward An Loc, the regiments the PAVN and the Front had kept in the U Minh forest came out against the outposts of Chuong Thien and Kien Giang. Historically this is where the offensive reached the Delta's countryside: dozens of posts lost, districts cut off, and the government's figures for its own security falling for the first time since 1968.

### Loc Ninh and the siege of An Loc
*7 Apr – 18 Jun 1972 · Loc Ninh and An Loc, Binh Long Province, on Route 13 · P5 · changed from history · EV000-76*

On 5 April the 5th Division of the PAVN B-2 Front attacked Loc Ninh, on Route 13 near the Cambodian border, and overran it on the afternoon of 7 April; the 9th Division took the Quan Loi base camp that evening, and the 7th Division cut Route 13 south of An Loc at the Tau O bridge with its 141st, 165th and 209th Regiments. An Loc, the provincial capital 100 km north of Saigon, was cut off by 8 April²⁹.

### Tan Canh, Dak To and the battle of Kontum
*24 Apr – 9 Jun 1972 · Tan Canh, Dak To, Ben Het and Kontum city, Kontum Province · P5 · changed from history · EV000-77*

In the Central Highlands the PAVN 320th Division began pressing the firebases on Rocket Ridge in early April, and on 24 April the 2nd Division's 1st and 66th Regiments, with the D10 Sapper Battalion and tanks, overran the ARVN bases at Tan Canh and Dak To II, held by the 42nd and 47th Regiments of the 22nd Division; the division "ceased to exist as a fighting unit", and its commander, Colonel Le Duc Dat, disappeared³⁰. Tan Canh fell in a day, to tanks and infantry already inside the wire before dawn, and nothing in the J reached a fight of that kind³¹.

### The fall of Quang Tri
*27 Apr – 2 May 1972 · Quang Tri City and Highway 1 south to the My Chanh River · P5 · changed from history · EV000-78*

On 27 April the PAVN renewed its attack on the 3rd Division's defence of Quang Tri City. Contradictory orders from the I Corps commander, Lieutenant General Hoang Xuan Lam, and from Giai left units moving in opposite directions, and on 1 May Giai ordered the city abandoned³².

### Resolution 21 and the North's rebuilding
*Oct 1973 – 1974 · Hanoi; the Laotian panhandle and the western Highlands · P6 · changed from history · EV000-87*

In October 1973 the 21st Plenum of the Party Central Committee in Hanoi resolved that the revolution in the South must continue by the path of revolutionary violence, and that the PAVN should respond to Saigon's operations and prepare for a decisive offensive. The PAVN rebuilt through 1973 and 1974: it improved the strategic road along the western side of South Vietnam east of the Truong Son, extended the fuel pipeline into the South, built up stocks of ammunition and armour in the base areas and grouped its divisions into army corps, the 1st Corps in October 1973 and the 4th Corps on 20 J

### The rice war of Chuong Thien
*15 Mar – 30 Jun 1974 · Long My, Kien Hung and Kien Thien Districts, Chuong Thien Province; the U Minh edge of An Xuyen; Binh Thuy air base · P6 · new · EV015-8*

The campaign was the Front's own and it had an author. In February 1974 the Military Region 9 Party Committee, short of rice after a 1973 harvest it had not been able to tax and with its main-force regiments living on half rations in the U Minh, decided on its own reckoning, before Hanoi's directives for the year reached it, to open a campaign against the posts of Chuong Thien in the dry season: to take the posts that guarded the canals, collect the spring harvest in the villages behind them, and feed its regiments to the monsoon².

### The war of attrition of 1974
*16 May – 10 Dec 1974 · The Iron Triangle; Thuong Duc, Duc Duc and Phu Loc in I Corps · P6 · changed from history · EV000-91*

From May 1974 the PAVN took the initiative with a series of "strategic raids" designed to grind down the ARVN and test its reserves. In III Corps the PAVN 9th Division attacked Rach Bap in the Iron Triangle from 16 May; the ARVN retook it only in November³³.

### The fall of Phuoc Long
*12 Dec 1974 – 6 Jan 1975 · Phuoc Long Province (Phuoc Binh and Song Be), III Corps · P6 · changed from history · EV000-92*

On 12 December 1974 the PAVN 4th Corps under Hoang Cam, with the 7th Division, the new 3rd Division and independent regiments including the 141st, 165th, 201st and 271st, and two armoured companies with 14 T-54s, attacked Phuoc Long Province on the Cambodian border. It was defended mainly by Regional Force battalions, reinforced by the 1st and 2nd Battalions, 7th Regiment and the 1st Battalion, 9th Regiment of the 5th Division and the 81st Airborne Ranger Battalion³⁴.

### The defence of I Corps
*13 Mar – 18 Apr 1975 · Quang Tri, Hue, Quang Ngai, Quang Tin and Da Nang · P6 · changed from history · EV000-94*

Historically, on 13 March Thieu ordered Truong to give up most of I Corps and withdrew the Airborne Division towards Saigon as a reserve; on 20 March he ordered him to hold only Da Nang; on 29 March he ordered him to turn back and retake it, which Truong refused³⁵. The contradictory orders, given as the PAVN 2nd Corps with the 304th, 324th and 325th Divisions attacked from the north and west and the 2nd Division and 52nd Brigade struck in Quang Ngai and Quang Tin, broke I Corps; Hue was abandoned on 25 March, about 6,000 soldiers of the 2nd Division deserted on 28 March, and the PAVN enter

### The battle for the Highlands
*14 Mar – 19 Apr 1975 · Pleiku and Kontum; Phuoc An on Route 21; Route 19 through the Mang Yang pass to An Khe · P6 · changed from history · EV000-95*

Historically, on 14 March at Cam Ranh, Thieu ordered Phu to abandon Pleiku and Kontum and pull II Corps back to the coast; the chief of the Joint General Staff, General Cao Van Vien, warned against Route 19 because of the French disaster at the Mang Yang Pass in 1954, and Thieu chose Route 7, a disused road in poor condition³⁶. The retreat was ordered verbally and kept secret; some 400,000 civilians joined the columns, the PAVN ambushed them near Cheo Reo, and only the 6th Ranger Battalion and the 19th Armoured Cavalry Squadron arrived in good order; an estimated 155,000 civilians were kil

### The Politburo's calendar: Saigon after the rains
*25 Mar – 14 Apr 1975 · Hanoi and the roads south · P6 · changed from history · EVMT01-4*

Historically the date of the fall of Saigon was set in Hanoi between 25 March and 14 April, and it was set by the rains and by the road. On 25 March, with Hue abandoned and the Highlands column destroyed, the Politburo resolved to take Saigon before the rainy season, which in the southern provinces begins in May and turns the lowlands around the capital to mud; on 31 March, with Da Nang taken, it decided to do it in April; and on 14 April it named the operation the Ho Chi Minh Campaign.

### Operation SOUTHERN WALL and the rains
*1 May – 31 Dec 1975 · Da Nang, Qui Nhon and the central coast; Saigon; Hanoi and the strategic road · P6 · new · EV011-3*

The Republic that entered the rains of 1975 had lost the Highlands, Quang Tri, Thua Thien, Quang Ngai, Quang Tin and Phuoc Long, about a third of its army's infantry and most of the heavy equipment of II Corps and the 1st and 2nd Divisions; it held III and IV Corps whole, Da Nang and the Quang Nam lowlands, and the coast from Qui Nhon south³⁷. Its general reserve, the Airborne and Marine Divisions, was at Da Nang, five hundred kilometres from the capital the next offensive would aim at.

## Settled positions about the enemy

- **POSTNA-3** · vars: ENEMY.engagement_control, ENEMY.regeneration, SANCT.laos, SANCT.cambodia · While the enemy controls whether to accept battle and regenerates in sanctuary, attrition has no crossover point; a strategy that waits for one waits for something the geometry does not permit (TNA G-8)
- **POS001-3** · vars: HANOI.will · Reform that erodes the Front's base raises Hanoi's urgency and shifts the arguments inside the Politburo; it does not change Hanoi's commitment to armed reunification or the timing of its decisions to invade (001 §2 F001-12; §4.P2)
- **POS001-4** · vars: POP.gvn_legitimacy, VCI.strength · A one-band gain in the countryside's allegiance does not carry into the conventional battles of 1972 and 1975; the end state turns on the military balance after the American withdrawal, and political gains are necessary but not sufficient to move it (001 §4.N)
- **POS004-1** · vars: RFPF.effectiveness, POP.night_control, ENEMY.engagement_control · Infantry small arms change how the fights the enemy accepts go, never which fights he accepts; at the outpost their value equals the platoon's presence after dark and the reaction behind it, and the enemy's answer to a better-armed post is to attack what is not rearmed (004 F004-1, F004-3, F004-16; §4.P1)
- **POS005-3** · vars: ENEMY.engagement_control, FIX.capability · In this war from Khe Sanh onward the PAVN does not lay a set-piece siege to a position the Americans can measure, until the conventional offensive of 1972 forces it to besiege An Loc and Kontum; it loses that one way of choosing its battles while the B-52J and the coordinate cell are present, and regains it when they leave in 1973 (005 §4.P3, §4.P5; EV000-41, EV000-76, EV000-77)
- **POS006-1** · vars: FIND.vci, VCI.strength, POP.night_control · Phung Hoang adds the layer above the hamlet to what the Special Branch knows, only where the night is held; outside the held belt it is the historical Phoenix whatever its rules, and its audited count, which falls where it works best, is the measure, never its arrest count (006 F006-15, F006-18, F006-26)
- **POS006-2** · vars: US.unit_quality, US.casualties, ENEMY.engagement_control · Unit rotation makes the American battalion fight better in the contacts it gets and changes neither which contacts it gets nor the late-war breakdown of discipline; it gives the enemy a relief window to aim at, and it does not prevent atrocity (006 F006-6, F006-16, F006-19)
- **POS007-1** · vars: ARVN.leadership, ARVN.effectiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · In this war the ARVN's battalions from 1965–67 are commanded by officers a board chose on written criteria and two raters' reports, for eighteen months, with relief for cause; this puts ARVN effectiveness at the cap of the bands in 1966–68, and the enemy answers by declining the better battalion and attacking the unreformed unit beside it, so the gain appears as battalions not lost rather than in any metric (007 §4.P2; EV007-2, EV007-3)
- **REVMT01-1** · reverses POS001-3 · vars: HANOI.will, ENEMY.engagement_control, PAVN.strength_south · Hanoi's commitment to armed reunification is fixed throughout and nothing in the force reaches it; the timing of its offensives is not fixed, and the schedule of the last campaign in particular was set week by week by the ARVN's behaviour in 1975 (the plan for 1976 accelerated after Phuoc Long and again after the Highlands, EV000-92); a memorandum that changes the ARVN, the PAVN's losses or the Republic's state on the eve of the offensive must test what it does to that schedule (MT01 M-6, M-10, M-12)
- **POSMT01-2** · vars: PAVN.strength_south, ENEMY.regeneration · In this war the PAVN's killed and wounded in 1972 were about a tenth above the historical figure, concentrated in the 5th, 7th, 9th, 320th and 2nd Divisions at An Loc and Kontum; the North replaced the men within its 1973 flow and formed its corps on the historical dates, so the extra loss cost the 1974–75 divisions quality and not time (MT01 M-1; EV000-87)
- **POSMT01-3** · vars: HANOI.will, PAVN.strength_south, ARVN.effectiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · The date of the Republic's fall, 30 April 1975 within a window of about 27 April to the first days of May, is derived and not carried: it was set by Hanoi's resolution of 25 March to finish before the rains and by the 1st Corps' march, and only a delay of about three weeks or more in the collapse of I and II Corps would have moved it, by putting the assault into the rains; better ARVN units act on fights the PAVN bypasses and do not reach that threshold (MT01 M-12; EVMT01-4, EV000-96)
- **POSMT01-4** · vars: POP.night_control, VCI.strength, POP.gvn_legitimacy, FIND.vci · The countryside at the end of 1972 is not history's: where a PAVN division sat in the peopled lowlands (northern Binh Dinh, Quang Tri) the gains of 1964–71 were lost, while the held belt of the Delta and the Saigon region kept its posts and files and stays one band better at night and against the infrastructure; the government's legitimacy returns to history's through the decrees of 1972 (MT01 M-4; EVMT01-1, EVMT01-2, EVMT01-3)
- **POS008-2** · vars: POP.night_control, RFPF.effectiveness, STRIKE.responsiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · A radio kept on the air at the post supplies the means of calling help in POSTNA-2 and moves the post's binding constraint to the reaction and fire within range; the Front answers by attacking the relief and the posts that cannot call, and the radio's gain appears as attacks not made (008 §2 F008-1, F008-3, F008-6, F008-16)
- **POS008-3** · vars: ARVN.self_sufficiency, US.political_tolerance, HANOI.will · In this war the Republic's own arsenal and battery works stretched the fiscal 1975 appropriation to about $850 million–$1 billion of history's and kept its ammunition and communications from going dark in 1974, but delayed the collapse of I and II Corps by days, not the three weeks that would have moved the date; domestic sustainment without an air arm the Republic owns and a choice of corps commanders does not move the rung (008 §4.P6, §4.N; EV000-89, EVMT01-4)
- **POS009-1** · vars: ARVN.effectiveness, RFPF.effectiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · Basic training changes how the fights the enemy accepts go and how many wounded live after them, never which fights he accepts; in this war the ARVN of 1964–65 stands a band above history on the course, the carbine and the educated lieutenant together, and the enemy answers the trained soldier with the mine, the sapper and the untrained target (009 §4.P1, §4.P2; EV002-2, EV009-2, EV009-4)
- **POS009-3** · vars: ARVN.desertion, ECON.inflation, VCI.strength · Training does not reach desertion, which follows the soldier's pay, rice and family; the trained deserter carries the course home, and a few hundred a year in the Saigon belt carry it to the Front's guerrillas (009 §4.P2; EV009-3)
- **POS010-1** · vars: ARVN.effectiveness, RFPF.effectiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · In this war every RVNAF and territorial NCO since 1957 has passed the course for his grade, and empty squads are given to corporals first class who passed the leader's course; this changes how squads and posts fight the fights the enemy accepts, never which fights he accepts, and the enemy answers by passing the units that keep the routine and attacking those that do not, so the gain appears as companies not destroyed and posts not attacked (010 F010-19, F010-25; EV010-3, EV010-4)
- **POSCP02-1** · vars: ARVN.effectiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · In this war the ARVN battalion of 1966–68 stands at the cap of the bands through four memoranda (007, 009, 010 and 004 before them), and the battalions broken in 1966–67 are about two-fifths to a half fewer than history's, a judgment whose factors overlap and whose upper bound is the "about half" of 010; any further provision on the battalion is measured in that running sum and not in the band, and none of it changes which fights the enemy accepts (CP02 §3, §5)
- **POSCP02-2** · vars: ENEMY.engagement_control, POP.civilian_harm, VCI.strength · Every provision since 004 that improved the RVNAF below the company was answered by the enemy moving his war to what the provision did not reach: the relief, the borrowed district, the mine in the hamlet, the untrained self-defence group; the provisions' gain in the army is paid for in part by the unprotected population, and every later provision touching the army or the posts names the target the enemy moves to and estimates the cost there (CP02 §1, §6; EV008-4, EV009-2, EV009-4, EV010-4)
- **REVR01-1** · reverses POSCP02-1 · vars: ARVN.effectiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · The judgment of POSCP02-1 on the war stands: the ARVN battalions broken in 1966–67 are about two-fifths to a half fewer than history's, a judgment whose factors overlap and whose upper bound is the "about half" of 010, and none of it changes which fights the enemy accepts. What is reversed is its method: further provisions on the ARVN battalion are no longer measured outside the variable because the variable is capped. They are measured on the v1.0.6 scale, in the range of ARVN effectiveness and the facet they act on, and the running sum feeds that range (R01)
- **REV011-1** · reverses POSMT01-3 · vars: HANOI.will, PAVN.strength_south, ARVN.effectiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · The method of POSMT01-3 stands: the date of the fall is derived from Hanoi's calendar, and only a delay of about three weeks or more in the collapse of I and II Corps moves it. What is reversed is the date. In this war the collapse came three to five weeks late, because Thieu gave no withdrawal order on 13–14 March 1975; the Politburo put the assault on Saigon back to the dry season of 1975–76, and the fall is expected between February and May 1976 (011; EVMT01-4, EV000-94, EV000-95)
- **POS012-1** · vars: VCI.strength, FIND.vci, POP.night_control · In this war a combined interagency task force with lift, raid teams and cross-province warrants from 1964 broke the Front's district government of the held belt from its edge in 1965–67, about a third to a half of the district layer in 12–18 provinces beyond what the police and the district centres had done; it reached committees beyond the held belt only as far as helicopter and warrant, never into the base areas, and its gains hold only where the posts hold the night (012 F012-27; EV012-4)
- **POS013-1** · vars: AIR.north_effect, TRAIL.tonnage_arriving, HANOI.will · In this war the air campaign against the North was run from Saigon from 2 March 1965 on the theater's own list, without zones around Hanoi or Haiphong and without pauses, and opened with a strike that destroyed the North's power, bulk fuel, great bridges, jet base and Haiphong's cranes in a week; it did not reduce the flow to the South beyond the record's trace, and it did not move Hanoi's will; the restrictions on bombing the North were never the war's binding constraint (013 F013-7, F013-18; EV013-1, EV013-3)
- **POSCP03-1** · vars: STRIKE.responsiveness, PAVN.strength_south, TRAIL.tonnage_arriving · The unrestricted opening of the air war against the North in March 1965 disrupted the North's economy, air force and alliances more than any other act of the war and did not reach the war in the South: the South's needs were small, carried through Laos by labour, and the North replaced fuel and power with drums and diesels in a season, while the trucks Moscow sent in place of heavy plant went to the Trail. The divisions held at home in 1965 were the North's home-defence divisions on history's course too, and no formation reaches the South late by more than weeks (CP03 §5, the user's question of 25 Nov 2026)
- **POSCP03-2** · vars: FIND.vci, ENEMY.engagement_control · A picture of the enemy's political organisation warns of where his political apparatus will act and not of when or in what strength his main forces will; at Tet 1968 the files held the caches, committees and guides of the uprising, the combined estimate read them as local, and MACV's judgment of the main effort and the Joint General Staff's leave order absorbed the warning, so the surprise was national and the change was confined to the corps centres of III and IV Corps (EV000-42, EV012-8; the user's question of 25 Nov 2026)
- **POSCP03-3** · vars: POP.night_control, VCI.strength, FIND.vci · Night control judged by corps in units for the first time: the land, the police, the posts and the task force hold about 8–14 points more of III Corps' and 6–12 points more of IV Corps' rural people after dark than history's by the end of 1967, about six months to a year ahead of history's pacification there, and about 3–9 points more at the end of 1974; I and II Corps never move more than a few points, and those two corps decided 1972 and 1975 (CP03 §8; the user's question of 25 Nov 2026)
- **POS014-1** · vars: FIND.vci, VCI.strength, SANCT.cambodia · In this war a night raid force on the Front's senior apparatus from 1964 drove that apparatus out of the provinces it administered and across the Cambodian border by 1967, where no allied instrument could reach it; the raid force's falling yield from 1967 measures that success and not its failure, and the displacement is never reported as a reduction in the Front's organisation (014 §4.P2, F014-19, F014-21; EV014-5, EV014-7)
- **POS015-3** · vars: RFPF.effectiveness, POP.night_control, STRIKE.responsiveness, ENEMY.engagement_control · In this war from 1964 the Front does not assault a covered post on a clear night within the gunship net, and it moves its night attacks to the monsoon cloud, to the posts beyond the net and into the hamlets; on the coast of I and II Corps the monsoon nights are the Front's until the VNAF's radar gunships cover them from 1969 (015 EV015-1, EV015-2, EV015-4)
